title: Paracelsus
description: Published in 1835 and praised by Wordsworth, Hazlitt and the actor Macready; a dramatic poem on the Renaissance alchemist Paracelsus, whose pursuit of knowledge is set against the claims of love and of common life.
plot_or_argument: Paracelsus seeks universal knowledge and neglects his friends Festus and Michal; he achieves fame as a healer, is denounced, fails, and dies acknowledging that he has missed the truth by seeking it apart from human love, in a death scene of reconciliation.
narrative_structure: A play in acts in blank verse, with the lyrical interludes and choruses set in shorter lines and in rhyme.
literary_form: Verse drama in eleven scenes (closet drama)
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic text. Verse drama in blank verse: the unrhymed iambic pentameter carries the dialogue, with lyrical interludes in shorter lines and in rhyme for songs, choruses and set pieces. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
historical_context: The 1830s vogue for the Renaissance (Bulwer's novels, Carlyle's lectures), the Victorian debate about the claims of knowledge against feeling, and Browning's own ambition to be a poet of the intellectual life.
literary_significance: Paracelsus made Browning's name among the critics and established the Renaissance as his imaginative territory; its theme of the knowledge-seeker who fails through pride is the matrix of the later monologues from 'A Grammarian's Funeral' to 'Andrea del Sarto'.

title: Sordello
description: Published in 1840 and the most notoriously difficult poem of the century — Tennyson said he could make nothing of it, and Browning's readers could not follow its syntax: a poem on the thirteenth-century troubadour Sordello and the politics of Lombardy.
plot_or_argument: Sordello, a poet of Mantua, seeks fame and love; he becomes involved in the Guelf-Ghibelline struggle over the succession of the emperor Frederick II, betrays his trust, and dies in obscurity, having learned that the poet's true work is to make the world's will conscious.
narrative_structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
principal_characters: Sordello; Palma (Cunizza); Taurello Salinguerra; Ecelin da Romano; Adelaide; Naddo; Eglamor
literary_form: Long narrative poem in blank verse
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. The dialogue or narrative runs in blank verse, the unrhymed iambic pentameter. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
historical_context: The Italian communes of the thirteenth century, Dante's Purgatorio (where Sordello appears), and the Victorian interest in Italian history and in the poet's political role. The record dates the work as composed between 1839 and 1840 and first published in 1840 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice, it is catalogued under idyll and domestic narrative poem; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
literary_significance: Sordello is the extreme case of Browning's difficult middle style, and its failure in the market taught him to write for the voice and for the dramatic moment rather than for the reader of narrative. Its theory of the poet's social function is the philosophical key to his later work.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1840, as long narrative poem in blank verse, by Robert Browning. Composed between 1839 and 1840. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Pippa Passes
description: The first of the Bells and Pomegranates pamphlets, published in 1841: a dramatic poem in four episodes, in which the silk-winder Pippa's songs, overheard by the people of Asolo, change the course of their lives.
plot_or_argument: Pippa, a poor girl of Asolo, is given one holiday a year; her innocent songs, sung as she passes, wake remorse in the adulterous murderers Ottima and Sebald, save the sculptor Jules's marriage to the girl he was tricked into wedding, send the young patriot Luigi to his mission, and move the Monsignor to foil a plot to sell Pippa herself into prostitution. The four episodes follow her through one New Year's Day, from morning to night.
narrative_structure: A play in acts in blank verse, with the lyrical interludes and choruses set in shorter lines and in rhyme.
principal_characters: Pippa; Ottima and Sebald; Jules and Phene; Luigi and his mother; the Monsignor; the Intendant; Bluphocks
literary_form: Verse drama (dramatic poem with four episodes)
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic text. Verse drama in blank verse: the unrhymed iambic pentameter carries the dialogue, with lyrical interludes in shorter lines and in rhyme for songs, choruses and set pieces. The form is the ode, in irregular or regular stanzas. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
historical_context: The 1840s and the Victorian idealisation of the pure redeeming woman; the Italian town of Asolo; and the pamphlet form of Bells and Pomegranates, sold cheaply to reach a new public. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1841 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice, it is catalogued under victorian verse drama and revived tragedy; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
literary_significance: Pippa Passes is the most lyrical of Browning's early works and the one in which his faith in the power of art and undesigning goodness is stated most directly; 'The year's at the spring' became one of the best-known Victorian lyrics, and the structure of overheard song influencing action is a technical invention of lasting interest.

bibliographical_notes: Published by Edward Moxon in September 1841 as the third number of Bells and Pomegranates; the series of eight pamphlet numbers ran from 1841 to 1846 and carried most of the author's early drama. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Dramatic Lyrics
description: Published in 1842 as the third Bells and Pomegranates pamphlet and containing 'My Last Duchess', 'Soliloquy of the Spanish Cloister', 'Porphyria's Lover' and 'Johannes Agricola in Meditation': the founding collection of the English dramatic monologue.
plot_or_argument: Each poem is spoken by a dramatic character at a moment of revelation: the Duke of Ferrara exhibits his last duchess's portrait and reveals that he had her killed; the Spanish monk reveals his hatred in the very cadence of his prayer; Porphyria's lover strangles her and is sure God has not said a word.
narrative_structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.
principal_characters: the Duke of Ferrara ('My Last Duchess'); the monk ('Soliloquy of the Spanish Cloister'); Porphyria's lover; the Pied Piper of Hamelin; Count Gismond; Waring
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
historical_context: The 1842 pamphlet market, the Victorian fascination with the Italian Renaissance, and the religious revival and its pathologies (the 'madhouse cells' of the two first poems). The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1842 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.
literary_significance: Dramatic Lyrics is the collection in which the English dramatic monologue became a distinct genre; 'My Last Duchess' is the most anthologised English poem of the century, and the collection's technique of letting a speaker condemn himself by his own rhetoric is the foundation of the modern poetic exploitation of dramatic voice.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1842, as collection of dramatic lyrics, by Robert Browning. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Men and Women
description: Published in two volumes in 1855 and a commercial failure — thirteen months after publication 244 copies had been sold — and now regarded as the greatest single volume of Victorian poetry: containing 'Fra Lippo Lippi', 'Andrea del Sarto', 'Bishop Blougram's Apology', 'Cleon', 'Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came', 'A Toccata of Galuppi's' and 'Love Among the Ruins'.
plot_or_argument: The poems are a gallery of speakers — Renaissance painters, a Greek philosopher, an Elizabethan lover, a bishop, a Roman patrician, a Venetian musician's listener — each caught at the moment when his view of life is revealed as inadequate or heroic. 'Fra Lippo Lippi' defends the flesh against asceticism, 'Andrea del Sarto' is the painter who could do everything but the one thing, 'Bishop Blougram' is the worldly churchman who argues that doubt is a luxury only the faithful can afford.
narrative_structure: The work is in 51 poems. It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
principal_characters: Fra Lippo Lippi; Andrea del Sarto and his wife Lucrezia; Bishop Blougram and Gigadibs; Karshish; Cleon; Childe Roland; the Grammarian ('A Grammarian's Funeral'); Galuppi ('A Toccata of Galuppi's'); the speaker of 'Love among the Ruins'
literary_form: Poetry collection in two volumes (51 poems)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
historical_context: The Florence of the 1850s and the Brownings' Italian life, the Victorian crisis of faith and its Catholic and sceptical answers, and the art criticism of the period (Vasari's Lives newly available to English readers).
literary_significance: Men and Women is the central volume of Victorian poetry after In Memoriam: it invented the modern poetic anthology piece, and its speakers' arguments about art, faith and the flesh are the source of the Victorian poetic drama of ideas. Pound, Eliot and the modernist dramatic lyric are inconceivable without it.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Chapman and Hall in two volumes in November 1855; it is the collection in which the dramatic monologue, 'Fra Lippo Lippi', 'Andrea del Sarto', 'Bishop Blougram's Apology', establishes itself as the author's characteristic form. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Dramatis Personae
description: Published in May 1864 and the volume that reversed Browning's neglect, selling 1,700 copies in the first year: containing 'Rabbi Ben Ezra', 'Caliban upon Setebos', 'Mr Sludge, The Medium', 'Abt Vogler', 'Prospice' and 'James Lee's Wife'.
plot_or_argument: The poems range from Caliban's grotesque theology to the spiritualist medium Mr Sludge's self-exposure, from the Rabbi's affirmation of age and love to the widower's defiance of death in 'Prospice'; the collection is organized around the theme of the soul's relation to God and to the beloved.
narrative_structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
principal_characters: Caliban and his god Setebos; Mr Sludge, 'the Medium'; Rabbi Ben Ezra; Abt Vogler; St John ('A Death in the Desert'); James Lee's wife; the speaker of 'Prospice'; Gold Hair, the girl of Pornic
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
historical_context: The 1860s, the death of Elizabeth Barrett Browning in 1861 (which shapes 'Prospice' and 'James Lee's Wife'), the vogue of spiritualism in London, and the Oxford Movement's aftermath in the debate on faith.
literary_significance: Dramatis Personae made Browning famous in his own lifetime and contains the poems by which the Victorian religious sensibility is best known; 'Caliban upon Setebos' is the great Victorian poetic treatment of natural theology, and 'Rabbi Ben Ezra' the age's most quoted defence of the imperfect life.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1864, as poetry collection, by Robert Browning. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Ring and the Book
description: Published in four volumes in 1868-69 and the longest and most ambitious of Browning's poems: the story of a Roman murder trial of 1698, retold twelve times by the different people involved, until the reader has to weigh the versions.
plot_or_argument: Count Guido Franceschini, a poor nobleman of Arezzo, marries Pompilia, the supposed daughter of the Roman couple Pietro and Violante Comparini, and takes her to Arezzo, where she is mistreated and flees towards Rome with the priest Giuseppe Caponsacchi; Guido pursues and murders her and her parents, and is tried and executed. The twelve books give the story in the voices of half Rome, the other half Rome, the tertiary, the murderer, the murdered wife, the young priest, the Pope, and finally the poet's own book.
narrative_structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
principal_characters: Count Guido Franceschini; Pompilia; Giuseppe Caponsacchi; Pietro and Violante Comparini; Pope Innocent XII; Dominus Hyacinthus de Archangelis; Johannes-Baptista Bottinius; Half-Rome; the Other Half-Rome; Tertium Quid
literary_form: Epic-length narrative poem in twelve books, in blank verse
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The dialogue or narrative runs in blank verse, the unrhymed iambic pentameter. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
historical_context: The Old Yellow Book, a printed record of the 1698 trial that Browning bought in a Florence market in 1860, the Italian legal system of the seventeenth century, and the Victorian interest in casuistry and in the relativity of evidence.
literary_significance: The Ring and the Book is the Victorian age's one true epic and the fullest treatment in English of truth as a product of multiple perspectives; its structure anticipates the modernist impersonal narrative (Eliot, Pound, Joyce) and its dramatic psychology is unmatched in Victorian poetry.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Smith, Elder in four volumes issued monthly from November 1868 to February 1869; the poem was written in Florence and Rome between 1864 and 1868 and is the longest poem in English by its line count. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Pied Piper of Hamelin; A Child's Story
alternative_titles: Pied Piper of Hamelin; A Child's Story
description: Written for the son of the actor William Macready in 1842 and published in the Hood's Magazine and in the Bells and Pomegranates series the same year: the best-known English retelling of the medieval legend.
plot_or_argument: The town of Hamelin is infested with rats; a mysterious piper offers to remove them for a reward, does so with his music, and is refused payment; he returns and pipes away the children of the town, all but one lame boy who is left behind.
narrative_structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
principal_characters: the Pied Piper; the Mayor of Hamelin; the Corporation; the lame boy left behind; the children of Hamelin; the rat who survives to tell the tale
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
historical_context: The medieval German legend (attested from the thirteenth century), the Victorian children's book market, and the 1840s interest in folk narrative that produced the Grimms' Tales in translation. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1842 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
literary_significance: The Pied Piper is one of the founding poems of English children's literature and the version in which most English-speakers know the legend; its moral about the consequences of bad faith gave the story its Victorian currency as a parable of the social contract.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in Dramatic Lyrics (1842), the second number of Bells and Pomegranates, issued by Edward Moxon in May 1842. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Seraphim, and Other Poems
description: Published in 1838 when she was thirty-two: the title poem is a Greek-style drama on the angels who watch the Crucifixion, together with 'The Romaunt of Margaret', 'The Poet's Vow' and the ballads that show the influence of the Greek dramatists she had studied since childhood.
plot_or_argument: The Seraphim stages the angels who witness the Crucifixion and cannot understand God's purpose; the poem is a chorus-driven drama of grief and prophecy. The shorter poems are ballads, romances and meditations on art and the poet's vocation.
narrative_structure: A play in acts in blank verse, with the lyrical interludes and choruses set in shorter lines and in rhyme.
principal_characters: Ador and Zerah, the seraphs ('The Seraphim')
literary_form: Verse drama and poems; victorian verse drama
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic text. Verse drama in blank verse: the unrhymed iambic pentameter carries the dialogue, with lyrical interludes in shorter lines and in rhyme for songs, choruses and set pieces. The author's characteristic manner is blank verse of sustained narrative drive.
historical_context: The 1830s, her reading of Aeschylus and the Greek tragedians, the Italian exile of her father's political sympathies, and the provincial religious culture of Herefordshire. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1838 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under victorian verse drama and revived tragedy; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
literary_significance: The Seraphim made her name and shows the classical and prophetic ambition of her early art; it is the volume in which the woman poet claims the Greek dramatic form, and its critical reception opened the way to her appointment as a leading poet of the 1840s.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Elizabeth Barrett Moulton-Barrett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1838, as verse drama and poems, by Elizabeth Barrett Browning. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Poems (1844)
description: Published in 1844 and the volume that made her famous: containing 'The Cry of the Children', 'Lady Geraldine's Courtship', 'The Dead Pan', 'Bertha in the Lane' and the first of the sonnets to Robert Browning.
plot_or_argument: 'The Cry of the Children' is a protest against child labour in the mines and factories, written in the metre of a report of the Children's Employment Commission; 'Lady Geraldine's Courtship' is a narrative romance; 'The Dead Pan' narrates the death of the pagan gods; the sonnets record the love that had not yet been spoken.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is blank verse of sustained narrative drive.
historical_context: The 1844 report of the Children's Employment Commission, the repeal of the Corn Laws (1846), the anti-slavery movement, and her reading of the Greek and Hebrew poets. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1844 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
literary_significance: Poems of 1844 is the volume in which the Victorian woman poet became a public political voice; 'The Cry of the Children' is the most famous English poem on child labour, and the volume's reception (and its correspondence with Browning) made it the turning point of her life.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Elizabeth Barrett Moulton-Barrett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1844, as poetry collection in two volumes, by Elizabeth Barrett Browning. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Sonnets from the Portuguese
description: Forty-four Petrarchan sonnets written in 1845-46 during the courtship and published in 1850, with the pretence of being translated 'from the Portuguese': the greatest English sonnet sequence of the century by a woman, and the founding text of the Victorian love lyric.
plot_or_argument: The sequence moves from the speaker's disbelief that she can be loved, through the growth of love and the fear of losing it, to the marriage and the giving of the child; the central sonnet, 'How do I love thee? Let me count the ways', follows 'I never gave a lock of hair away' and precedes the closing sonnets of renewed devotion.
narrative_structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The form is the fourteen-line sonnet. The author's characteristic manner is blank verse of sustained narrative drive.
historical_context: The 1845-46 courtship at 50 Wimpole Street, the invalid's seclusion, and the Victorian conventions of the love sonnet, which had been modelled on Petrarch and on the masculine sequence since Wyatt. The record dates the work as composed between 1845 and 1846 and first published in 1850 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
literary_significance: Sonnets from the Portuguese gave English poetry its central sequence of reciprocal love and reversed the gender of the Petrarchan tradition: the beloved speaks. 'How do I love thee' is among the most quoted poems in the language, and the sequence is a founding text for the study of Victorian women's writing.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Elizabeth Barrett Moulton-Barrett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1850, as sonnet sequence, 44 sonnets (petrarchan), by Elizabeth Barrett Browning. Composed between 1845 and 1846. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Casa Guidi Windows
description: Published in 1851 and written in the apartment in Florence whose windows look on the streets of the 1847-49 revolution: a poem in two parts on Italian liberty, the failure of the 1848-49 risings and the continued hope of the Risorgimento.
plot_or_argument: Part I records the civic festivals of 1847 and the hopes of an Italian nation; Part II, written after the defeat of the Roman Republic and the flight of the Grand Duke, refuses despair and calls on the Italian people to renew the struggle.
narrative_structure: A single poem, read as one continuous whole from its opening to its close.
literary_form: Two-part political poem in blank verse
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The dialogue or narrative runs in blank verse, the unrhymed iambic pentameter. The author's characteristic manner is blank verse of sustained narrative drive.
historical_context: The 1847-49 Italian revolutions, the flight of Grand Duke Leopold II from Florence, the fall of the Roman Republic in 1849, and the English liberal sympathy for Italy that shaped the Brownings' Florentine years.
literary_significance: Casa Guidi Windows is the finest English poem of the Italian Risorgimento and a major political statement by a woman poet; it broke with the Victorian convention that women's poetry should be domestic and established the public, prophetic voice that Murat and the later poets of liberation emulated.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Elizabeth Barrett Moulton-Barrett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1851, as two-part political poem in blank verse, by Elizabeth Barrett Browning. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Aurora Leigh
description: Published in November 1856 and the great Victorian poem on the woman artist: the autobiography of a poet, Aurora Leigh, from her childhood in Italy to her mature work and love, and a sustained argument for women's access to art and to meaning.
plot_or_argument: Aurora, orphaned in Florence, is brought up in England by her Puritan aunt, refuses the proposal of her cousin Romney Leigh (who is to be a social reformer), goes to London to write, and publishes her book; Romney's socialist schemes at Leigh Hall fail (the burning of the hall and the death of the people in it), he is blinded, and the novel ends with their marriage on the basis of her art and his repentance.
narrative_structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.
principal_characters: Aurora Leigh; Romney Leigh; Marian Erle; Lady Waldemar; the aunt; Vincent Carrington; Lord Howe
literary_form: Verse novel in nine books, in blank verse
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse, with a median line of eleven or twelve syllables and an unusually free handling of the iambic base, suited to narrative and argument.
historical_context: The 1850s: the woman question, the 'surplus women' census of 1851, the reforming philanthropies of the 1840s, the position of the woman writer in a market dominated by men, and the Italian exiles of London and Florence.
literary_significance: Aurora Leigh is the first English verse novel by a woman and the central literary argument of the Victorian feminist movement; its heroine is a professional artist, its plot refuses the marriage-ending until the woman has become the equal partner, and its treatment of the social problems of the 1840s (prostitution, poverty, the reformer's failure) is unusually direct. Virginia Woolf's account of it in Second Common Reader (1925) is the standard critical point of departure.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Elizabeth Barrett Moulton-Barrett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1856, as verse novel in nine books, in blank verse, by Elizabeth Barrett Browning. Composed between 1853 and 1856. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Poems before Congress
description: Published in 1860 and dedicated to the Italian exile and patriot Giuseppe Garibaldi: five poems on the politics of Europe in 1859-60 and the independence of Italy, the most openly polemical of Barrett Browning's volumes.
plot_or_argument: The poems celebrate Napoleon III's intervention in the Italian war of 1859 and lament the truce of Villafranca, in poems such as 'Napoleon III in Italy', 'A Tale of Villafranca' and 'A Court Lady'; 'A Curse for a Nation', the volume's best-known poem, was originally written for an American abolitionist society against slavery.
narrative_structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is blank verse of sustained narrative drive.
historical_context: The Anglo-French war with Austria, the unification of Italy under Victor Emmanuel and Garibaldi's expedition of 1860, and the anti-slavery agitation in Britain and America. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1860 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; idyll and domestic narrative poem.

title: The Battle of Marathon: A Poem

plot_or_argument: The poem narrates the Persian invasion, the Athenian appeal to Sparta, the Marathon campaign and the victory, with speeches of the Athenian generals and a providential interpretation of the Greek success.

title: The Bothie of Toper-na-Fuosich: A Long-Vacation Pastoral

title: Amours de Voyage

title: Dipsychus

title: The Latest Decalogue
description: Published posthumously in 1862: a ten-couplet parody of the Ten Commandments that reduces each to its commercial and social equivalent, and the most quoted Victorian epigram. It is a verse work of 1862 by Arthur Hugh Clough; it belongs to The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice and it is catalogued here under Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule.
plot_or_argument: Each couplet restates a commandment in the language of Victorian respectability and self-interest: 'Thou shalt not kill; but needst not strive / Officiously to keep alive'; 'Thou shalt not steal; an empty feat, / When it's so lucrative to cheat'.
narrative_structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The verse runs in rhymed couplets. The author's characteristic manner is hexameter and loose, conversational rhymed forms.

title: Mari Magno

title: The Strayed Reveller, and Other Poems
description: Published anonymously in 1849 as the work of 'A', and the volume that contains 'The Forsaken Merman', 'Mycerinus', 'The Sick King in Bokhara' and 'Resignation': the poetry of withdrawal, of the classical mask and of resignation before the world.
plot_or_argument: 'The Strayed Reveller' is a dialogue between the young reveller and Circe, in which the poet's vision is purchased by exclusion from action; 'The Forsaken Merman' is a ballad of a sea-creature's wife who leaves him for her church; 'Mycerinus' is the Egyptian king who learns that he has only six years to live and turns them into pleasure.
narrative_structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
principal_characters: the Youth, the strayed reveller; Circe; Ulysses; the Forsaken Merman and his children; Margaret, his human wife; Mycerinus
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The author's characteristic manner is classical plainness of diction and a limited, repeated vocabulary.

title: Empedocles on Etna, and Other Poems
description: Published anonymously in 1852 with 'Tristram and Iseult', 'The Scholar-Gipsy' (added in 1853), 'Memorial Versions' and the 'Switzerland' lyrics, including 'To Marguerite'. The title poem was withdrawn by Arnold from the 1853 collection.
plot_or_argument: Empedocles, the Sicilian philosopher, has lost the power to think and act; he converses with Pausanias and with Callicles, whose songs celebrate the world he can no longer enter, and climbs Etna to throw himself into the crater. The lyrics 'Tristram and Iseult', 'The Buried Life' and 'To Marguerite' dramatise the same estrangement in modern English terms.
narrative_structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

title: Poems (1853)
description: Published in 1853 under Arnold's own name, with the famous Preface on the choice of subjects, and reissued in a second series in 1855: the collection that made him the poet of Victorian doubt and the critic of the age.

title: Sohrab and Rustum
description: Published in the 1853 Poems and generally regarded as Arnold's finest narrative poem: a story from the Persian epic the Shahnameh, in which a father unknowingly kills his son in single combat. It is a verse work of 1853 by Matthew Arnold; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Epic and the Long Philosophical Poem and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Rustum, the Persian hero, has a son Sohrab by the princess Tahminah; Sohrab, seeking his father, joins the Tartar army and challenges the Persian champion, and in the duel Rustum wounds him mortally before discovering the truth. The poem ends with the father's grief on the banks of the Oxus.
